newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Van Miert warns on sports broadcasting rules.
newsitem.headline: Van Miert warns on sports broadcasting rules.

text.p: Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said on Thursday he was increasingly concerned about a handful of private media giants using their power to buy exclusive sports-broadcasting rights.
He told the European Parliament the Commission would insist on allowing the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), a grouping of public television channels, to negotiate similar rights for its members.

Responding to a challenge by private broadcasters, the European Court of First Instance ruled in July that a former Commission decision effectively exempting EBU from competition rules had not been properly drafted.
But Van Miert said that the Commission would now readopt its decision, bearing in mind the court's ruling.

"We are currently carrying out an in-depth assessment of the Court's decision but we think that as to the substance there is no reason to change our decision," Van Miert told the parliament's economic and monetary committee.

"There is this trend which seriously worries us that increasingly a few large groups can buy such rights," Van Miert said. He added that it seemed only fair that public broadcasters unite themselves to face media tycoons such as Rupert Murdoch and Leo Kirch.
In July, Germany's Kirch group won a bidding battle for television rights to the 2002 and 2006 World Cup Soccer Finals.
In his address to the parliament, Van Miert -- an enthousiastic soccer fan -- also warned European soccer governing body UEFA about its broadcasting rules.
"We think UEFA conditions are to strict," Van Miert said adding that the Commissin had received complaints.
"We are in discussions with UEFA, but if there is no progress we will have to act," he said.
He did not elaborate, but Commission officials said the complaints had been filed by television channels which broadcast UEFA matches but do not have exclusivity rights.

Van Miert also made it known that he had problems with plans by the Dutch football association KNVB to grant seven years' of exclusive broadcasting to sports channel Sport 7 in which it is a shareholder.
"Seven years is too long," Van Miert told the Economic and Monetary affairs commitee.
He hinted that the Commissison might ask KNVB to reduce the period to five years -- as was decided for a similar case involving British TV channel BSkyB.
KNVB notified the Commission in August of its plan to grant Sports 7 exclusive rights to broadcast Dutch premier league football matches.
There is no deadline for the Commission to come to a decision on the matter, but it usually informs companies of its preliminary finds within two months of notification.
Other shareholders in Sports 7 include Dutch powerful groups Philips Electronics NV, ING NV and publishing company Endemol.
Van Miert said that when assessing the case, the Commission would make a distinction between regular sports events and exceptional ones such as the Olympic Games.
